articles.title: The Need for Co-created Digital Health Capacity Building and Policy Implementation Across Africa
articles.dek: Why capacity building and policy for digital health work best when African institutions shape them from the start.
articles.fr: Pourquoi le renforcement des capacités et les politiques de santé numérique fonctionnent mieux quand les institutions africaines les conçoivent dès le départ.
articles.body:
![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PoL1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbf495c0a-8879-4262-8c42-6afdf748ebbc_1378x775.png)

***Guest Contributor Spotlight***

*Digital health transformation requires more than technology. It takes people, local expertise, and policies that translate into action.*

*In this edition of Digital Health Digest,* **[Dr Albert Attom](https://www.linkedin.com/in/drattom/)** *explores the need for co-created digital health capacity building and effective policy implementation across Africa, drawing attention to the importance of strengthening local capabilities and building sustainable digital health systems.*

*We are pleased to feature his perspective.*

---

In 2024, just 10 regional healthcare facilities in Ghana’s Volta Region were connected to a centralised call centre. Today, that number is 200. More than 1.6 million people are now benefiting from a more connected, more efficient health service, and 100% of staff at Ho Teaching Hospital can access Ghana’s Health Information Management System (GHIMS).

None of this happened because someone installed new software. It happened because we put healthcare workers at the centre of their own learning journey. This is the story of how research, training and co-created policy came together, and why I believe co-created capacity building is the missing piece in Africa’s digital health transformation.

## The technology is available. So why is no one using it?

Across emerging economies, governments and healthcare organisations want to adopt digital healthcare. The ambition is everywhere: electronic records, real-time data, connected facilities, digital supply chains. And increasingly, the technology is available.

But the systems to implement it are difficult. Again and again, I have seen digital tools purchased, installed and then left largely unused. Not because they do not work, but because the people expected to use them are reluctant to do so. The technology arrives. The adoption does not.

## What the research revealed

Our research at Ho Teaching Hospital set out to understand why healthcare workers were not using the technology available to them. The answers were not about the technology itself. They were about people, processes and preparation: for example, limited training, reliance on self-directed learning, workload pressures, and a perception that new systems added administrative burden rather than reducing it.

Once we understood the hurdles, the next question became obvious: what could be done to overcome them, and who should be designing the solution?

## From hurdles to co-created training

Based on the research, we developed a programme of training and capacity building built around the realities healthcare workers described to us, rather than what a system vendor assumed they needed. The hospital serves over 1 million people, so the programme had to be practical, role-specific and grounded in everyday workflows.

This is where my philosophy of impact research comes in. Rather than simply studying healthcare systems, we worked alongside clinicians, managers and policymakers to design the policy, train staff and help put the changes into practice. As I explained when the results were announced:

> *“Our aim was never simply to introduce new technology. It was to help healthcare professionals spend less time dealing with administrative processes and more time caring for patients.”*

## From training feedback to co-created policy

The feedback from the training became the foundation for something bigger. Working with staff and leadership, we co-created a healthcare digitalisation policy and helped the organisation to implement it. The result was Ho Teaching Hospital’s first Healthcare Digitalisation Policy, which the hospital’s Chief Executive described as “a major strategic milestone” that continues to guide investment in technology and service improvement.

Because healthcare workers helped shape the policy, they owned it. That ownership is what turns a document on a shelf into a change in everyday practice.

## The evidence: what changed

The combination of research, training and policy development delivered evidenced outcomes for staff, patients and the wider health system. Connected facilities rose from 10 to 200. Every member of staff gained access to GHIMS. Medicines and medical supplies are now managed more effectively, staff can monitor bed availability in real time, and information flows more easily across the hospital and the wider health service. A 2026 implementation review found that the partnership delivered impact “beyond academia”, strengthening workforce capability, improving organisational efficiency and enhancing patient care.

Most importantly, it changed the way people work. Worlase Dotse, a Nurse Specialist in Emergency Care, put it this way:

> *“The combination of participating in the research, contributing to policy development and undertaking the training has changed the way I work. I have observed positive changes through improved access to patient information, better communication between departments and more efficient processes.”*

Simon Yao Dzokoto, Director of Research, Policy Planning, Monitoring and Evaluation at Ho Teaching Hospital, added:

> “In my view, many of these developments would not have occurred in the same way or within the same timeframe without the support, expertise and engagement provided by Dr Albert Attom and Loughborough University.”

The work has also been recognised at the highest level. Ghana’s President John Dramani Mahama noted that international partnerships with academic institutions like Loughborough University are vital in achieving sustainable development and shared prosperity. There is more to do, particularly in telemedicine, electronic prescribing and artificial intelligence, but the foundations for long-term improvement across the region are now firmly in place.

## Introducing the Co-created Healthcare Policy and Practice Implementation Framework

Success at Ho Teaching Hospital raised an important question: how do we make this repeatable? My answer is a new framework, the Co-created Healthcare Policy and Practice Implementation Framework.

The framework is grounded in the established Knowledge-to-Action (KTA) approach developed by Graham et al. (2006), which connects knowledge creation with an iterative cycle of local adaptation, assessment of implementation barriers, tailored intervention delivery, evaluation and sustained knowledge use. Building on these principles, the framework incorporates explicit stages for stakeholder co-creation, policy development, workforce training and organisational facilitation, providing a structured approach to translating research into healthcare policy and practice (Graham et al., 2006; Field et al., 2014).

It moves through nine stages, from defining the problem to sustaining and extending what works:

![Article content](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gSyp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F77150f7d-eab7-4ec8-8441-a8a683bac1a9_1094x1000.png)

## What this means for healthcare leaders and practitioners

**Start with people, not platforms.** Before investing in new systems, find out why existing ones are not being used. The barriers are rarely technical.

**Co-create, do not impose.** Healthcare workers who help design training and policy are far more likely to adopt the change and sustain it.

**Connect research, training and policy.** Meaningful and sustainable change is achieved through interconnectivity. Each element strengthens the others; on their own, each falls short.

**Plan for sustainment from day one.** Embed responsibilities in routine budgets, induction, supervision and governance so that progress outlasts the project.

### Work with me

**[Dr Albert Attom](https://www.linkedin.com/in/drattom/)**

If your organisation is investing in digital health but struggling to see adoption, I would like to hear from you. I work with hospitals, health ministries, training institutions and development partners across Africa to co-create capacity building programmes and digitalisation policies, and to apply the Co-created Healthcare Policy and Practice Implementation Framework in real settings. Let us build healthcare systems that are more connected, more efficient and better equipped to meet the needs of the people they serve.

---

***About Digital Health Digest***

*Digital Health Digest features insights, ideas, and practical experiences from the people shaping digital health across Africa and beyond.*

*Are you working on a digital health initiative, policy, or innovation that deserves a wider audience? We welcome contributions from practitioners, researchers, policymakers, and innovators.*

***Interested in contributing?** Follow Digital Health Digest on Substack and subscribe to our newsletter for more expert perspectives and developments in digital health.*

Read the full story from Loughborough University: **[https://www.lboro.ac.uk/media-centre/press-releases/2026/october/loughborough-research-ghana-hospitals-improve-care/](https://www.lboro.ac.uk/media-centre/press-releases/2026/october/loughborough-research-ghana-hospitals-improve-care/)**

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!wqI2!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa1c307c3-cfe9-40af-af56-e830b9c1203c_860x837.png)

Three years ago, asking whether FHIR would become the dominant health data exchange standard was a legitimate debate. Today, 80% of countries with electronic health data regulations specifically mandate or advise FHIR, up from 56% in 2023. The debate is over. The implementation challenge is not.

Governments on every continent are writing FHIR into law, building national implementation guides, and setting compliance deadlines. What is actually driving this convergence, and what does it mean for the countries and institutions still figuring out where to start?

### The regulatory wave

The United States set the pace. The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule requires Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid programs, and Qualified Health Plan issuers to implement FHIR-based APIs for electronic health data exchange, with key requirements taking effect January 1, 2026. The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) pushes further: by July 2026, participating networks must expose data via FHIR APIs aligned with the US Core Implementation Guide and USCDI v3.

Europe followed with a bolder structural move. The European Health Data Space (EHDS) Regulation, which entered into force in March 2025, mandates the European Electronic Health Record Exchange Format (EEHRxF) built on FHIR specifications as a legal requirement across all EU member states. Implementing acts expected by March 2027 will define precise technical and semantic requirements for compliance. In November 2025, HL7 Europe published three new FHIR Implementation Guides covering R4, R5, and Extensions, giving member states a harmonized technical baseline.

Saudi Arabia and Estonia are enforcing national deadlines for FHIR integration. India’s Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission adopted FHIR for its health data exchange layer. Australia’s My Health Record ecosystem runs on FHIR. The pattern is consistent: governments are choosing FHIR not because of technical elegance alone, but because no alternative offers the same combination of open licensing, vendor neutrality, and a global community maintaining the standard.

### Why FHIR is winning the standards race

Previous health data standards required organizations to agree on entire message structures before exchanging a single data element. FHIR flipped this model. Its resource-based architecture lets systems exchange discrete, well-defined data objects (a Patient, an Observation, a MedicationRequest) over standard web protocols. A developer who knows REST APIs already understands 80% of how FHIR works.

This design choice reduced the barrier to entry dramatically. HL7 v2 dominated for decades because it was already deployed, not because it was easy to implement. FHIR is winning because it is both deployable and implementable by a broader workforce.

WHO recognized this advantage and positioned FHIR as the foundation for its SMART Guidelines initiative, which translates clinical recommendations into machine-readable, executable digital health content. The ambition: a country implementing WHO’s immunization guidelines should be able to deploy a FHIR-based decision support module directly into its health information systems, without rebuilding from scratch.

### The enforcement gap

Here is where the global picture gets complicated. While 80% of countries with regulations reference FHIR, the gap between policy intent and operational reality remains wide.

A 2025 survey by HL7 International found only 11 respondents reporting financial penalties for non-compliance with FHIR mandates, even among the 37 countries with published compliance deadlines. The mandates exist. The enforcement teeth, in most places, do not.

This gap is especially visible in Africa. Countries including South Africa, Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda, Ghana, and Nigeria have explicitly prioritized interoperability through national eHealth strategies aligned with HL7 and FHIR frameworks. The “Africa on FHIR” initiative, led by HELINA in collaboration with Africa CDC, HL7 International, and WHO, is building capacity for FHIR adoption across the continent. The Africa Standards and Interoperability Lab (SIL-Africa), hosted in Rwanda, supports development, testing, and scaling of interoperable digital health solutions.

The challenge: many national strategies lack detailed implementation roadmaps, financing mechanisms, and workforce investment plans. Countries are investing in digital health solutions while facing system fragmentation, limited interoperability, and a shortage of professionals trained in FHIR. The policy commitment is real. The implementation pipeline is thin.

### What FHIR R6 changes

The next version of the standard, FHIR R6, is expected to publish in late 2026 or 2027. Its first normative ballot opened in January 2026, with a second ballot opening July 2026.

R6 represents a maturity milestone. It moves the majority of commonly used clinical and administrative resources to normative status, meaning once you build against R6 normative resources, those APIs will not face breaking changes in subsequent releases. For organizations delaying adoption while waiting for stability, R6 removes their strongest argument for waiting.

R6 also introduces a new publishing model: immature resources move out of the core specification into incubator implementation guides, keeping the core lean and stable. Backward compatibility with R4’s normative resources is an explicit design goal, so a valid R4 Patient resource remains processable by an R6 server without modification.

For countries building their first national implementation guides today, R6 offers a more stable foundation than any previous release.

### What this means for decision makers

If you are leading digital health strategy at a national or institutional level, three realities demand your attention.

First, FHIR adoption is no longer optional for any country planning to participate in cross-border health data exchange. The EU, the U.S., and major economies across Asia and the Middle East have made their choice. Countries without FHIR strategies will find themselves isolated from the emerging global health data infrastructure.

Second, mandating FHIR in a national strategy document is necessary but insufficient. The countries making real progress are investing in three things simultaneously: national FHIR implementation guides tailored to their health system context, workforce development programs training developers and health informaticists in FHIR, and testing infrastructure (like SIL-Africa) where systems are validated against profiles before going live.

Third, the transition does not require replacing everything at once. FHIR-based integration between EMR systems and DHIS2 is already operational in Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, and South Africa. These implementations prove the model works in resource-constrained settings. Starting with a focused use case, patient registration, lab results exchange, or immunization reporting, and building outward is a more sustainable path than attempting a comprehensive interoperability overhaul.

### The road ahead

FHIR is becoming healthcare’s HTTP: a protocol so fundamental it fades into infrastructure. The question for health systems globally is not whether to adopt FHIR, but how fast they move from policy documents to running code.

The countries doing this well share a pattern. They pick a specific, high-value use case. They build a national implementation guide for it. They test it. They deploy it. Then they pick the next use case. No country has achieved universal FHIR-based interoperability overnight. Every country making progress started with one exchange working correctly.

The global push toward FHIR as the universal language of health data is real, funded, and accelerating. The remaining question is execution. And execution, as every implementer knows, is where the real work begins.

---

*Dr. Abel Mestie Mekonnen is a physician and digital health strategist specializing in health information systems interoperability across Africa. He serves as a Public Health Informatics Fellow at Africa CDC.*

*Subscribe to Digital Health Digest for practical insights on building health systems that work at scale.*

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!smdC!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa9a35ee5-568b-4005-9384-d8ea994759fb_2730x1536.png)

*It is not a shortage of doctors. It is a shortage of clinicians, managers, and policymakers who understand artificial intelligence.*

A district health officer in a rural setting opens a new dashboard. It recommends which patients to prioritize for follow-up this week. She asks the obvious question. How does it decide? Nobody in the room knows.

This scene is playing out across the continent. AI tools are arriving in African health systems faster than the workforce being asked to use them, govern them, and trust them.

The gap is real. It is widening. And the next decade of African digital health will be decided by who closes it first.

## The shift nobody is naming

Africa has spent two decades building a digital health foundation. Electronic medical records. District Health Information Systems. Interoperability frameworks. Health Information Exchanges. Much of this work is unfinished, but the direction is set.

What changed in the last 24 months is the arrival of AI at the point of decision. Triage algorithms. Predictive analytics for outbreak detection. Generative AI for clinical documentation. Decision support for drug dosing. Automated medical imaging review. Large language models drafting ministry reports.

None of this was in the workforce training pipeline five years ago. Most of it is not in the pipeline today.

> *The arrival of AI in African health systems is outpacing the workforce being asked to deploy it, govern it, and trust it.*

## Why this is a workforce crisis, not a technology crisis

When people discuss AI in African health, the conversation usually circles the same topics. Data quality. Infrastructure. Local language models. Regulatory frameworks. These matter. But they are not the binding constraint.

The binding constraint is people.

Consider what AI-ready health systems actually require:

- Clinicians who know when to trust an algorithm and when to override it.
- Public health officers who can read a model’s confidence interval and ask the right second question.
- Ministry staff who can write a procurement spec that includes bias testing, not just accuracy.
- Data scientists who understand the clinical workflows they are trying to improve.
- Facility managers who know what data protection looks like when the model vendor is in another country.

Almost none of this is taught in African medical schools, public health programs, or health management training. The curriculum has not caught up with the tools.

This is what a workforce crisis looks like. Not empty posts. Empty competencies.

## The closing window

There is a narrow window to act. AI adoption in health is following a familiar curve. Quiet pilots first. Then a few high-profile deployments. Then sudden scale-up driven by donor funding, vendor pressure, or political urgency.

Once scale-up begins, the workforce gap becomes invisible. People use tools they do not understand. Decisions get made by algorithms nobody audited. Bad outcomes get blamed on “the system.” Trust erodes quietly.

We have seen this movie before. The early DHIS2 rollout suffered from it. So did the first generation of facility EMRs. AI will suffer from it worse, because the tools are harder to interrogate and the consequences of getting it wrong land directly on patients.

*The question is no longer whether AI will shape African health systems. It is whether the people inside those systems will shape AI back.*

### What AI literacy actually means.

AI literacy is not about becoming a data scientist. It is not about coding. It is a layered competency that different roles need at different depths.

### Foundational (every health worker)

How AI systems are built at a high level. What training data is. Why models fail in populations they were not trained on. What algorithmic bias looks like in practice. How to read a model output with appropriate skepticism. When to call for human review.

### Applied (digital health professionals, clinicians using AI tools)

How to evaluate an AI tool before deployment. How to interpret performance metrics beyond accuracy. How to set up monitoring for model drift. How to integrate AI outputs into existing clinical workflows without creating new harm.

### Strategic (policymakers, ministry leaders, senior implementers)

How to write AI procurement specifications. How to build governance frameworks that fit African contexts. How to assess vendor claims. How to protect patient data when models are hosted externally. How to make equity a design requirement, not an afterthought.

The content exists. Most of it is free. The problem is not availability. It is curation and commitment.

## Seven courses that close the gap

Here is a starting shelf. Every course below is free to audit. All are accessible from anywhere in Africa with a laptop and a connection. Together they cover the three layers of AI literacy described above.

1. Ethics and Governance of AI for Health - OpenWHO | 3.5 hours | Free certificate The foundation. Built from WHO’s 2021 guidance on AI ethics in health. **[https://lnkd.in/esmaBQPq2](https://lnkd.in/esmaBQPq2)**.
2. AI in Healthcare Specialization - Stanford University via Coursera | 5 courses | Audit free The gold standard. Covers clinical data, machine learning fundamentals, AI evaluation frameworks, and a capstone. Apply for financial aid if you want the certificate. **[https://lnkd.in/dQjrWPPZ3](https://lnkd.in/dQjrWPPZ3)**.
3. Introduction to AI and Machine Learning in Healthcare - MGH Institute of Health Professions via edX | Audit freeFrom the clinical side. Strong on model training, validation, privacy, and real-world healthcare scenarios. **[https://lnkd.in/e3GhHmxk4](https://lnkd.in/e3GhHmxk4)**.
4. AI in Healthcare. Hype or Help? - via edX | Audit freeTeaches how real healthcare AI teams operate. **[https://lnkd.in/egdMB8kG5](https://lnkd.in/egdMB8kG5)**.
5. AI in Healthcare - Great Learning Academy | Self-paced | FreeA solid starter course. Covers AI fundamentals, generative AI, LLMs, ChatGPT applications in health, and ethical challenges. **[https://lnkd.in/esmuCSUH6](https://lnkd.in/esmuCSUH6)**.
6. AI Ethics for Beginners - Great Learning Academy | Self-paced | Free. Covers fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and human oversight. Strong on global frameworks including the EU AI Act. Essential context for anyone deploying AI in health. **[https://lnkd.in/eR5uGrKv7](https://lnkd.in/eR5uGrKv7)**.
7. Evaluations of AI Applications in Healthcare - Stanford Online via Coursera | Audit free | CME accredited. How to evaluate whether an AI tool actually works in your setting. Critical skill, often skipped. **[https://lnkd.in/eBcPEvcU](https://lnkd.in/eBcPEvcU)**

## A practical path

If you are a clinician, start with course 1, then course 3, then course 7. Roughly 20 hours over four weekends.

If you work in digital health implementation, start with course 1, then course 2, then course 4. Budget 40 to 50 hours across two to three months.

If you sit in a ministry or a donor agency making AI-related decisions, start with course 1, then course 6, then course 7. Roughly 15 to 20 hours. Finish within a month.

No single person needs all seven. An organization does.

*If every senior person at your organization finished three of these courses this quarter, you would be ahead of almost every African health institution deploying AI today.*

## The ask

Three things are worth doing this week.

First, forward this issue to one colleague who will use it. Someone on your team, someone you mentor, someone at a partner organization. AI literacy spreads fastest through trust.

Second, pick one course from the list and start it. The OpenWHO ethics course takes an afternoon. Finish it before Monday.

Third, raise AI literacy at your next leadership meeting. Not as a training line item. As a workforce strategy. Ask what percentage of your technical staff has completed a single structured course on AI in health. If the answer is zero, that is your starting point.

The question is no longer whether AI will shape African health systems. It is whether the people inside those systems will shape AI back. That requires competent people. Competent people require training. Training already exists.

All that remains is the decision to begin.

*If this issue helped you, forward it to one person. That is how the Digest grows.*

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!yxBc!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F162b8fbf-5cd3-42ae-b2ce-32c419867292_3264x1312.png)

*African clinicians are already using AI tools built in the US and Europe. Most of them use those tools carefully, as guides, not arbiters. And many of them know exactly why.*

Every month, a new AI tool lands in an African hospital with a press release and a pilot program. Chest X-ray interpretation. Malaria detection. Neonatal risk scoring. Some of these tools are genuinely impressive. A few of them are changing how care is delivered in facilities that have one doctor for every **[36,000 people in some rural counties.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5328402/)**

But here is what those press releases rarely say: the model was trained on data that did not come from those patients.

That gap, between where the training data came from and where the tool is deployed, is the defining challenge of AI in African healthcare right now. It is not a technology problem. It is a data sovereignty problem. And solving it requires a different conversation than the one we are currently having.

![Article content](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!UnWF!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Faf79faf5-545a-4123-b920-6b9250b61ade_797x277.png)

### What African Clinicians Already Know

In a 2025 study published through the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, researchers interviewed physicians and nurses across multiple African countries about how they use AI diagnostic tools. **[One physician from Mauritius](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3715275.3732160)** put it plainly: “All the software and medical devices we use have been developed in the USA or Europe. The outputs are indicative only and assist in formulating a preliminary diagnosis.”

That is not skepticism about AI. That is clinical judgment. Experienced practitioners know that a model trained on, say, imaging data from European hospitals will carry assumptions, about baseline anatomy, disease prevalence, comorbidity patterns, even equipment quality, that do not transfer cleanly to a district hospital in rural Ethiopia or southern Nigeria.

The problem compounds when you consider what the training datasets actually look like.

![Article content](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!N2H_!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F99962da0-8791-48fd-915e-94ac763b1fa9_797x323.png)

**[Less than 4%](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11823112/)** of the training data powering global medical AI comes from Africa, a continent that carries 25% of the world’s disease burden. This is not an oversight. It is the product of decades of underinvestment in African health data infrastructure, ethics review capacity, and the legal frameworks needed to share clinical data across borders safely.

The result: AI tools arrive in African health systems pre-loaded with someone else’s assumptions. The model may never have seen a case of sickle cell disease at the frequency it appears in West Africa. It may underperform on TB detection in patients with HIV coinfection at rates common in southern Africa. It may not account for the nutritional deficiency patterns that shape pediatric presentations across the Sahel.

These are not edge cases. They are the everyday clinical reality.

> The core issue is not whether AI works in African healthcare. It does, in specific, well-designed applications. The issue is who controls the data that defines what “works” means, and for whom.

### Three Things Africa Needs to Build, Not Buy

Acknowledging the data sovereignty problem is the easy part. The harder question is what it actually takes to fix it. In my view, three things need to happen in parallel.

**First, African health systems need federated clinical data infrastructure.** This means investing in the technical and legal architecture that allows clinical data to be used for model training without leaving national jurisdictions. Ethiopia’s Health Information Exchange, Ghana’s National Health Data Repository, and similar initiatives are early steps. They need policy teeth and long-term funding, neither of which should depend on a donor grant cycle.

**Second, AI governance frameworks need to be built from African clinical realities, not retrofitted from elsewhere.** The WHO’s AI for Health ethics guidance is a useful starting point. But African ministries of health need to localize these frameworks with specificity: who reviews AI tools before deployment? What validation evidence is required in African patient populations? Who bears liability when an AI recommendation leads to harm?

**Third, we need African-led AI model development, not only African deployment of external models.** Rwanda’s Mbaza NLP project, Lelapa AI in South Africa, and Masakhane’s work on African language models show what becomes possible when African researchers lead. These efforts need structured support from ministries, from Africa CDC, and from international partners willing to be co-investors rather than solution exporters.

![Article content](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iZKK!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ffd7df0bb-9b45-416e-8970-8ffb57f8a4ec_795x375.png)

### Optimistic, But Clear-Eyed

I am not pessimistic about AI in African healthcare. A community health worker in Siaya County diagnosing malaria in 90 minutes with a $50 microscope and a smartphone is a real story. An LLM quietly flagging drug interaction errors in a Nairobi clinic is a real story. These tools are extending clinical capacity in ways that training alone cannot match fast enough.

But optimism without clarity does a disservice to the patients these tools are supposed to serve. A diagnostic AI that performs brilliantly on American imaging data and mediocrely on Ethiopian patient presentations is not a neutral tool. It encodes a hierarchy of whose health data matters enough to train on.

Africa does not need to wait for better AI. It needs to build the conditions under which AI works for African patients on African terms. That means data infrastructure, governance frameworks, and African-led model development. And it means the international community treating African health data not as an extraction opportunity, but as something African systems should own, protect, and benefit from.

The technology is ready. The question is whether the systems around it are.

***“What would it take for your country to own its clinical AI ecosystem, not just use someone else’s?”***

I’m interested in what you’re seeing on the ground. If you work in digital health, health policy, or AI governance in Africa, I’d like to hear your perspective.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!X6L1!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fdd30304d-040f-4f41-91d6-ae0b7d0e8953_2752x1536.png)

Across our continent, digital health innovation is everywhere.

Most Ministries of Health can list more than ten digital health projects running at the same time, each with its own app, dashboard, server and donor report.

Yet when leadership asks a simple operational question, **“How many facilities submitted data last month?”,** the answer still requires phone calls, spreadsheets, and manual reconciliation.

This contradiction reveals a hard truth:

> Africa does not have a shortage of digital health solutions. It has a shortage of **national digital health systems**.

## The pilot paradox

Behind impressive slide decks and demo dashboards, too many digital health tools never move beyond:

- a pilot district
- a donor funding cycle
- a single champion within the ministry

This is often described as the “pilot graveyard.”

But pilots do not fail because of weak ideas or poor technology. They fail because **no system was ever designed to absorb them**.

Innovation without systems produces fragmentation, not scale.

## Fragmentation by design, not by accident

When each implementing partner brings its own:

- platform
- data model
- login credentials
- reporting workflow

the ministry inherits a **patchwork**, not a health information system.

Frontline workers are forced to juggle multiple applications that do not talk to each other. Data becomes siloed inside vertical programs. Digital tools increase workload instead of reducing it.

Procurement decisions often prioritize individual solutions rather than:

- national architecture
- interoperability standards
- long-term ownership

Even well-designed tools struggle to scale because they were never aligned to a shared national blueprint.

## The shift that matters: from projects to platforms

Through work shared via **Digital Health Digest** and advisory roles across African health systems, one pattern is consistent:

Countries that scale digital health successfully stop thinking in terms of *projects* and start building **platforms**.

This shift rests on three foundational pillars.

### Pillar 1: National architecture and standards

Every country needs a clear, government-owned digital health architecture that defines:

- core registries and shared services
- interoperability standards
- data exchange mechanisms

Without architecture, each new tool adds complexity instead of capability.

Architecture is not technical bureaucracy. It is **sovereignty over the health system’s digital future**.

### Pillar 2: Workforce and change management

Digital health does not fail because health workers resist technology.

It fails because systems are deployed without:

- training
- clear roles
- accountability
- incentives aligned to data quality

Scaling requires internal digital health capacity within government—not permanent reliance on vendors.

Ownership must sit inside institutions, not contracts.

### Pillar 3: Governance and sustainable financing

Pilots are funded as short-term projects. National systems must be funded as **long-term infrastructure**.

This means:

- multi-year budgeting
- clear data ownership and stewardship
- procurement rules that reward interoperability and reuse

If a system collapses when funding ends, it was never national to begin with.

## Practical steps governments can take now

Ministries do not need to start from scratch. They can repurpose existing investments by adopting a systems lens:

1. **Map and rationalize** the current digital health ecosystem
2. **Enforce interoperability** as a procurement requirement
3. **Treat EMRs and data exchange** as core infrastructure
4. **Build internal capability**, not long-term dependency

None of these require new technology. They require **leadership, coordination, and discipline**.

## Final reflection: pilots don’t fail and systems are never built

The difference between a digital health pilot and a national system is not innovation.

It is:

- architecture
- governance
- people

Our governments that treat digital health as **core public infrastructure**, planned, funded, and governed at the highest level, will be the ones that achieve real impact at scale.

### An invitation

If you lead or advise a:

- Ministry of Health
- regulatory authority
- regional health body

and are ready to move **from pilots to platforms**, this is the work explored through **Digital Health Digest** and advisory engagements.

For:

- keynote talks
- closed-door strategy sessions
- national digital health architecture workshops

feel free to connect via LinkedIn or through **[Digital Health Digest](https://www.linkedin.com/company/digital-health-digest-dhd/)**.

Let’s stop scaling pilots. Let’s start building systems.

articles.body:
I sometimes think about a map from 1854. A doctor named **John Snow** mapped a cholera outbreak in London. He wasn’t just treating sick people. He was looking at **data**. He traced the outbreak to a single dirty water pump. By closing that pump, he saved countless lives. Snow was one of the first people to prove that our health is tied to the environment around us. Today, we need a modern version of that map.

In 2000, **[close to 10 million children died](https://vizhub.healthdata.org/child-mortality)** before their fifth birthday. That number is now cut in half, thanks to huge investments in vaccines and basic health care. We solved that crisis by focusing on human health. But the next big health crisis will not be solved by doctors alone.

Here is a fact that should worry everyone. **[Three out of every four new infectious diseases in humans come from animals](https://www.cdc.gov/one-health/about/about-zoonotic-diseases.html#:~:text=Zoonotic%20diseases%20are%20very%20common,in%20people%20come%20from%20animals.).** Think about it. COVID-19, Ebola, Avian Flu. They all jumped from animals to people.

![Article content](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Hafw!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F32c4bb8c-ad3f-4a4b-8b04-5250bc7b6679_1017x1000.jpeg)

This is a stark reminder that human health, animal health, and environmental health are not separate things. They are deeply linked. This idea is called ***One Health.*** When we cut down forests, we bring people closer to new viruses in wildlife. When livestock get sick, that disease can jump to the farmer. When we pollute the water, it makes both people and animals ill.

The problem is that our defences against these threats are stuck in the past. We have human health systems. We have veterinary systems. We have environmental monitoring systems. They operate in silos. They do not talk to each other. When a cow gets a strange fever on a small farm, that data often stays with the local vet. It doesn’t get connected to global public health officials who could spot the start of a new outbreak.

The stakes are personal and global. A fragmented system means we are always reacting too late. It means a local illness in one corner of the world can quickly become a deadly, expensive global pandemic. We need a way to see the whole picture in real time. We need to create one unified health map of the planet.

## From Cholera Maps to AI-Driven Global Security

It may seem new, but the idea that health is connected has been around for centuries. What’s changed is how we watch and react to those connections.

Look at **John Snow’s** famous **1854 cholera map**. He carefully mapped the outbreak in London. Even though it was simple, it was an early way to use data for public health. It showed how a disease spread so people could stop it.

The modern **“One Health”** movement officially **[started in 2004 with the 12 Manhattan Principles](https://idpjournal.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s40249-022-00979-9#:~:text=In%20response%20to%20the%202002,with%20global%20epidemics%20%5B13%5D.)**. This document called for experts to work together. It urged scientists, policymakers, and doctors to stop working alone. The goal was to combine information about human, animal, and environmental health.

> The first digital steps were slow but promising.

In **2006**, three global organizations, **[FAO, WHO, and WOAH, created GLEWS](https://www.woah.org/app/uploads/2021/03/glews-tripartite-finalversion010206.pdf#:~:text=The%20Global%20Early%20Warning%20and%20Response%20System,and%20control%20of%20animal%20disease%20threats%2C%20including)**. This Global Early Warning System focused on watching animal diseases. It was an early digital effort to predict and respond to threats worldwide.

Around the late **2000s**, mobile phones became common. They quickly became important tools for reporting diseases and collecting data, especially in rural areas.

By **2009**, the **CDC** created its **One Health Office**. This showed a formal commitment by a major public health group to share data between human and animal health sectors.

The real digital growth started in the **2010s** and is still speeding up.

In the mid-**2010s**, mobile technology became advanced. Apps like **[AfyaData](https://afyadata.sacids.org/)** let communities report health events in real time. This gave valuable information about disease patterns and outbreaks.

As more data was collected, people demanded **FAIR data** in the late **2010s**. FAIR means data must be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. Collecting data wasn’t enough. To be useful, data had to be easy to find, understand, and combine across different systems.

Then came **AI**. It suddenly became part of everything we do. AI can analyze huge amounts of data. It promises to find patterns and predict outbreaks very accurately. AI’s potential to change One Health was obvious right away.

The **COVID-19 pandemic** in **2020** was the ultimate driver for change. It showed how vulnerable health systems are when they don’t share information. The pandemic forced more data sharing. It quickly increased the use of remote medicine and sped up the creation of quick digital response systems.

In **2021**, the **“[One Digital Health](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33492240/)“** framework was formally introduced. This brought the two powerful concepts together. The framework is a plan to use digital tools to support One Health goals. The aim is to create a more joined-up, strong, and fair approach to global health security.

## What’s Happening Now

The One Digital Health (ODH) framework is a guide. Think of it as a steering wheel. One Health and Digital Health are the keys that lead to better health for people, society, and nature. This framework covers many important areas.

These include talking with citizens, education, watching the environment, combining human and animal healthcare, and using new technologies in medicine.

**[Many groups are pushing ODH forward](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/one-health/ohhlep/ohhlep--one-health-theory-of-chance.pdf)**. The Quadripartite includes **[World Health Organization](https://www.linkedin.com/company/world-health-organization/)** , **[FAO](https://www.linkedin.com/company/fao/)** , WOAH, and UNEP. They are working together on several projects. Groups like the ODH Think Tank in Portugal are finding new ways to innovate. Universities like **[Cornell](https://www.vet.cornell.edu/giving/one-health)** and **[UZH](https://www.onehealth.uzh.ch/en.html)** are doing advanced research. Their work focuses on using AI for animal diagnosis and mixing different health data sources.

The technology for ODH is wide-ranging and active. Exciting real-world uses are appearing everywhere.

### Technology Examples

- **Eyes in the Sky and Smart Sensors Drones**, remote sensing, and environmental sensors are being used. They track things like deforestation and pollution. They also study how wildlife migrates. This gives valuable data on the health of natural systems.
- **AI as a Health Detective Platforms** like **[ProMED-mail and HealthMap](https://healthmap.org/promed/)** use AI. They predict disease outbreaks, like Ebola, avian flu, and COVID-19. They catch these diseases before they spread widely. This allows for quick action.
- **Wearables for All Smart** collars for pets and ear tags for farm animals are used now. They watch vital signs and behavior. This helps find sickness early and improves animal well-being./
- **Vet-on-Call Remote** healthcare is also for animals. Apps like **[iCow and VetAfrica](https://www.cojengo.com/2015/05/vetafrica-mobile-user-experience/)**00 give remote support. They help farmers and vets manage animal health.
- **Smart Cities and Healthy Coexistence** A study showed how smart medical devices can monitor a woman and her dog in a city. This system can predict possible health problems for both of them.

These digital tools create a huge amount of data. This data must follow the FAIR principles. It needs to be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. This ensures true collaboration. It lets us fully use the data to meet One Health goals.

## The Elephant in the Room

Even with huge potential, **One Digital Health (ODH)** faces big problems. We must solve these issues now.

### Data and Ethics

**Privacy versus progress** Collecting a lot of sensitive health data brings up hard questions. Who owns the data? How do we keep it secure and private? We need to balance the good that comes from this data against the need to protect people’s privacy. This debate is complex and never stops.

**The digital divide** Not everyone has a smartphone or good internet. Not everyone knows how to use digital tools. This lack of access creates a digital divide. It could prevent vulnerable people from getting the benefits of ODH. We must ensure fair access to digital tools and training for everyone.

**AI’s ethical risks** We rely more and more on **AI**. This raises worries about bias, fairness, and transparency. We must make sure **AI** systems are developed and used ethically. Their decisions must be understandable. We need to hold these systems accountable.

### Technical and Financial Hurdles

**Difficulty connecting systems** Human health, animal health, and environmental monitoring systems often work separately. Combining these different digital systems is a huge technical challenge. We need to create shared data rules and standards. This is the only way to make all systems work together smoothly.

**The cost problem** Building, setting up, and keeping up advanced digital systems costs a lot of money. We need to decide who pays for these big investments. We also need to make sure **ODH** projects can last a long time.

**Dealing with false information** Digital tools can spread true information quickly. However, they can also spread false health information. Fighting health misinformation is key. We must also teach people how to spot good information online. This is necessary to keep the public healthy.

The future of **One Digital Health (ODH)** is full of exciting possibilities. Here’s what we expect to see.

### Smarter AI and Faster Connections

**AI gets even better** We will see big steps in **AI** for health. This includes better diagnoses and personalized treatments for people and pets. **AI** models will also predict problems with more accuracy. They will forecast disease outbreaks, pollution levels, and the effects of climate change. **AI** will become a vital tool for protecting health and the environment.

**A hyper-connected world** New network tech like **5G** and **Wi-Fi 7** will enable seamless, real-time data flow. This will happen even in remote areas that don’t have good service now. Imagine a sensor in a far-off forest instantly sending updates to a city hospital.

### New Devices and Biotech

**Health monitoring everywhere** Wearable devices will become much more advanced. Tiny, simple patches will offer **“hospital-grade”** health readings. Medical devices will connect to the internet and blend into our homes, farms, and wild areas. This allows for constant checks on health and environmental conditions.

**Biotech breakthroughs** Advances in genetic engineering and stem cell research will transform things like disease resistance and treatments. They will also improve food security. These new molecular tools will help us solve global health problems.

### Systems and Sustainability

**Self-learning health systems** The main goal is to build dynamic systems. These systems will always collect, combine, and analyze data across the entire planet. They will constantly learn and improve their performance based on new information.

**Focus on a green economy** **ODH** will be key to tracking how we use resources and create waste. It will help us promote sustainable practices. This ensures that the digital technologies we use don’t hurt the environment themselves.

**Global fairness** We expect ongoing work to set up dedicated global rules. These rules will ensure fair access and responsible data sharing. The goal is to make sure everyone benefits from **ODH**, no matter where they live or how much money they have.

Which of these future possibilities, like AI diagnostics or hyper-connected systems—do you think will be the most impactful in the next five years?

## A Healthier Future for All

**One Digital Health (ODH)** changes everything about how we understand and manage health globally. It is not just a new trend in technology. It is a completely new way to think.

By linking people, animals, and the planet with smart digital tools, we can get ahead of diseases. We can protect different types of plants and animals. We can build a truly sustainable future for everyone.

This path has clear challenges. We face ethical issues, worries about privacy, and technical roadblocks. But we can succeed with careful planning and real teamwork. We must also always focus on fairness. If we do this, **ODH** offers the promise of a world that is healthier, stronger, and more equal for generations to come.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5Ajl!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F46a16745-ece2-4f31-9c59-701d39dbd8ec_1344x768.png)

Of all the memories from my years as a doctor, the ones that stick with me the most are the lines. I see the long line of mothers outside our small health center, sitting patiently under the acacia trees, babies on their backs, waiting for the single health officer on duty. I remember the crowded hallways of the primary hospital, the feeling of being overwhelmed, knowing that behind every face was a story, a family, and a fear that we, with our limited resources, might not be able to quell. This is the reality of healthcare for so many. But I believe we are on the verge of a revolution, one that can erase those lines and bring expertise to the most remote corners of our country.

### The AI Takeover: A Historical Look at Healthcare Tech

Let’s not labor under the illusion that AI is a recent arrival to the healthcare scene. Venture back to the 1970s, where “expert systems” like **[MYCIN](https://www.opentrain.ai/glossary/mycin#:~:text=Examples/Use%20Cases:,artificial%20intelligence%20and%20medical%20informatics.)** attempted to decipher the complexities of infectious diseases. These early iterations were cumbersome, rigidly rule-based, and ultimately failed to ignite a revolution within healthcare. Physicians were not supplanted by the monolithic mainframes of the era.

Fast forward to the dawn of the digital age, spanning the years 2000 to 2010. Propelled by the proliferation of data (hark, the advent of Electronic Health Records!) and the sophistication of algorithms (enter the realm of deep learning!), AI began to materialize as a tangible force. **[IBM Watson](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/genetics/articles/10.3389/fgene.2020.00200/full)** garnered considerable attention for its forays into cancer treatment, and, almost overnight, AI was outperforming human perception in the analysis of X-ray images. The prognostications shifted: AI was no longer envisioned as a replacement for physicians but rather as a means to ***augment*** their capabilities.

Now, in the epoch of generative AI and expansive language models, commencing in the 2020s and extending into the future, we find ourselves navigating uncharted waters. AI transcends mere analysis; it ***creates***, from the generation of synthetic medical images to the drafting of intricate clinical notes. This is, indubitably, a “disruptive force” of considerable magnitude.

### The Digital Doctor Will See You Now: Ed Marx’s Vision

**[Ed Marx](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/how-ai-redefining-traditional-care-edward-marx-wzrtc)**, an influential voice within the industry from Marx Advisory, raises a cautionary alarm. He posits that unless hospitals demonstrate adaptability, self-service AI applications will simply circumvent them. Patients are already availing themselves of symptom assessment tools and wellness applications, thereby diverting routine cases (and, consequently, revenue!) away from conventional healthcare providers.

But what, precisely, constitutes “self-service AI”?

- **Your Personal Health Concierge:** Envision AI-driven chatbots capable of conducting symptom evaluations, scheduling immediate appointments, and even formulating personalized treatment regimens.
- **Care Beyond Walls:** Marx envisions a future where “hospital-at-home” models and virtual care modalities become the norm, rendering healthcare more accessible and cost-effective.
- **The “Digital Front Door”:** Hospitals must cultivate intelligent online platforms that furnish rapid responses, telehealth services, and transparent pricing structures to retain patients within their networks.
- **Super-Personalized Medicine:** AI possesses the capacity to integrate your medical history with your genomic data, enabling the creation of exquisitely tailored treatments (as exemplified by the 95% effective tumor treatment).

### The Good, The Bad, and The AI

### Can We Really Trust an Algorithm with Our Lives?

- **Bias Alert:** AI’s learning is contingent upon data. If this data lacks diversity, the AI may perpetuate existing disparities in healthcare. What transpires if an algorithm designed for one demographic group misdiagnoses individuals from another?
- **Black Box Problem:** The decision-making processes of AI algorithms often remain opaque. This absence of transparency undermines trust and complicates the assignment of responsibility when errors occur. Who bears the burden of accountability?
- **Losing the “Human Touch”:** Can a machine truly possess empathy? Critics express concern that AI may erode the compassion and personal connection that are indispensable to the healing process.

### “Is My Data Safe?” - The Privacy Minefield:

- **Big Data, Big Risk:** AI necessitates access to vast quantities of sensitive health data, thereby amplifying the potential for breaches.
- **Anonymity? Think Again:** Even data that has undergone “anonymization” can frequently be re-identified. The data collected by your smartwatch, your telehealth consultations – all contribute to the insatiable appetite of the AI ecosystem.
- **Who Owns Your Health Story?:** When AI developers gain possession of your data, who exercises control over its utilization and commercialization?

### “Will a Robot Take My Job?”

- **Automation Anxiety:** Medical coders, transcriptionists, schedulers – repetitive tasks are undoubtedly within the crosshairs of AI-driven automation.
- **Augmentation, Not Replacement (Mostly):** Experts generally concur that AI will ***augment*** the majority of healthcare roles, thereby liberating human professionals to concentrate on more complex, empathetic, and critical-thinking tasks. However, retraining and upskilling initiatives are of paramount importance.

### The Silver Lining: How Hospitals Are Embracing the AI Future

**[Sarasota Memorial Health Care System](https://www.healthcareitnews.com/news/sarasota-memorials-predictive-ai-reduces-ed-boarding-hours-almost-third)** serves as a compelling success story, demonstrating that the integration of AI need not be a harbinger of doom. By employing predictive AI (”iQueue for Inpatient Flow”), the hospital achieved a remarkable 32% reduction in Emergency Department boarding times. This translates to diminished waiting periods, increased patient satisfaction, and enhanced operational efficiency.

### General Catalyst’s Bold Move

- **[A “Test Kitchen” for AI:](https://www.google.com/search?q=https://www.generalcatalyst.com/perspectives/announcing-our-definitive-agreement-for-a-strategic-partnership-with-summa-health)** The venture capital firm General Catalyst demonstrated its commitment to AI innovation by acquiring Summa Health, a health system, for over $500 million. The firm intends to transform Summa Health into a living laboratory for the integration of cutting-edge AI technologies (through their new company, Percepta) across all facets of hospital operations.
- **Enterprise-Wide Makeover:** Percepta’s ambitions extend beyond piecemeal improvements; the company aims to fundamentally redesign healthcare processes, fostering a synergistic relationship between human professionals and AI systems.
- **A Blueprint for the Future:** This acquisition serves as a potential archetype for how entire hospital systems can modernize their operations through the strategic deployment of AI.

### Adopt or Adapt: Strategies for a Human-Centered AI Future

- **Smart Investments:** Hospitals must allocate resources to AI initiatives, not as isolated projects, but as an integral component of their ongoing operational expenses.
- **Training Our Heroes:** Equipping physicians, nurses, and support staff with the skills necessary to effectively utilize AI, fostering a mindset of partnership rather than competition.
- **Design for Humans First:** AI should empower clinicians to devote ***more*** time to patient interaction, not less. Automating routine tasks to amplify the impact of human connection.
- **Ethics at the Forefront:** Implementing robust ethical guidelines, addressing biases, and ensuring transparency in AI-driven decisions. Patients must provide informed consent, fully cognizant of how their data is being utilized.
- **Measuring What Matters:** Beyond mere efficiency metrics, assessing patient satisfaction and emotional well-being.
- **The Hybrid Approach:** Preserving the virtues of traditional care (face-to-face interaction) while harnessing the benefits of AI (efficiency, personalized insights).

### The Road Ahead: What’s Next for AI in Healthcare?

- **Connected Care:** Expect seamless data exchange between physicians, insurers, and care facilities, culminating in extraordinarily precise and preventive medicine.
- **AI as Your Health Guardian:** AI will vigilantly monitor your lifestyle and clinical data to anticipate health risks (e.g., heart attack, diabetes) before they manifest as tangible issues.
- **Regulatory Scramble:** Governments are engaged in a high-stakes race to formulate regulations that strike a delicate equilibrium between innovation and safety, transparency, and equity.
- **Optimistic vs. Realistic:** While a utopian vision of AI resolving all healthcare challenges may captivate the imagination, a more pragmatic perspective acknowledges the ongoing challenges associated with data quality, regulatory frameworks, and cultural adaptations.
- **The Unstoppable March:** Whether hospitals embrace AI wholeheartedly or with reservations, its role in healthcare will inevitably expand, enriching domains spanning from surgical procedures to drug discovery and patient engagement. The objective is unequivocal: to harness AI’s capabilities to amplify human intelligence and ensure that care remains profoundly human.

### Conclusion

AI represents a formidable wave crashing upon the shores of traditional healthcare. It promises to deliver more affordable, faster, and personalized care, challenging established paradigms and catalyzing crucial discussions pertaining to ethics and employment. Simultaneously, it is emerging as a game-changing force for enhancing efficiency and fostering innovation.

The future of healthcare is not predicated upon AI ***replacing*** physicians but rather upon physicians and hospitals ***leveraging*** AI to forge a more intelligent, efficient, and, ultimately, a more human-centered experience for all. Are hospitals on alert? Assuredly. But, more importantly, they are evolving.

![](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Wo87!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6608609b-069d-4b6a-8281-f01fa5aba17f_2336x1760.png)

## A New Dawn for African Healthcare

Health care in much of Africa faces serious gaps. Many people live far from clinics, doctors are scarce, and disease rates remain high. Hospitals and health centers often struggle with limited staff and outdated tools. Artificial intelligence offers a way to close some of those gaps. AI can help doctors diagnose illnesses faster and more accurately, support community health workers in remote areas, and keep patient records organized. It can also help health systems plan resources, predict outbreaks, and manage supplies.

This isn’t just another piece of new technology. Used well, AI could change how health care works across the continent and bring quality care closer to people who need it most. But the path forward is complex. Infrastructure is uneven, data privacy rules are still taking shape, and training health workers to use new tools takes time and investment. The promise is real, but success will depend on careful planning and a focus on people as much as on machines.

## From Early Experiments to Today’s Digital Push

Artificial intelligence in Africa has deeper roots than many people think. Work began quietly in the 1980s with small medical AI projects. Kenya tested simple systems to guide patients through first questions before seeing a doctor. Egypt used early AI tools to help with eye care. Clinics in The Gambia tried computer programs to spot serious illnesses in rural areas. These were limited efforts, but they showed that technology could help reach people far from major hospitals.

Through the 1990s and early 2000s, AI stayed mostly in universities and research labs. Business uses, like fraud detection in South African banks and telecom companies., came before health care. Momentum grew again in the 2010s and took off during the COVID-19 pandemic. Lockdowns created a sudden need for remote care, contact tracing, and digital health records. At the same time, internet access expanded quickly, with roughly 160 million more Africans coming online between 2019 and 2022.

That mix of urgent need and better connectivity sparked a wave of homegrown health-tech start-ups. Across the continent, new teams began using AI, machine learning, and big data to build tools for African health systems, designed for local challenges and conditions. What started as a few small trials has become a broad movement that is still gathering speed.

## AI in Action Today

Artificial intelligence is moving from talk to practice in African health care. Many experts see it as a way to improve diagnosis, manage scarce resources, and make care more affordable. The need is clear: in some areas there are fewer than one doctor for every ten thousand people, and disease rates remain high. AI tools can help fill those gaps.

Across the continent, the work is varied. In Southern Africa, South Africa leads with AI X-rays that speed up TB screening, systems that predict staff shortages, tools to manage hospital beds, and apps that give patients personal health advice. In East Africa, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, and Zambia, AI supports cancer care, predicts antibiotic resistance, powers mobile health assistants like Dr Elsa, and runs chatbots such as Babylon Health to share birth information. Drone services like Zipline use AI to plan medical supply routes, and eye-screening programs catch diabetic retinopathy early.

West Africa is equally active. Nigeria has Ubenwa, which listens for signs of birth asphyxia in new-borns, Lola AI for menstrual tracking on WhatsApp, and LifeBank to manage blood and oxygen supplies. In North Africa and the wider MENA region, Egypt and Jordan are applying AI to manage diabetes, detect tumours early, and craft national AI health strategies.

Progress depends on collaboration. The Africa CDC’s digital health strategy sets direction, while groups like PATH use AI to forecast vaccine shortages. Local start-ups like HealthTraka, Mino Health AI Labs, and many others, are designing tools built for their own communities and health systems. The result is a growing network of projects turning AI’s promise into real services.

## Challenges and Concerns

AI can help health care in Africa, but big hurdles remain. The first is a shortage of local data. AI systems learn from large, high-quality datasets, yet many African countries have limited records or inconsistent reporting. Models trained on patients in Europe or North America may not work well for African populations and can introduce bias.

Infrastructure is another barrier. Many rural clinics still face weak internet connections and unreliable electricity. Even when the tools exist, they can’t run without steady power and a solid network. A lack of skilled people adds to the problem. There are too few AI specialists, data scientists, and health workers with digital training, and many leave for higher-paying jobs abroad.

Ethics and safety are also critical. Health data must be protected from misuse and cyberattacks. Some AI systems are “black boxes,” making it hard to explain how they reach a diagnosis. If an automated chatbot gives poor advice, who is responsible? New tools could also deepen inequality if they reach only city hospitals while rural areas fall further behind.

Another worry is outside control. Much of the technology and funding comes from abroad, raising concerns about “digital colonialism” and whether Western rules for AI ethics fit African cultures and needs. And a larger question lingers: can AI fix weak hospitals, low pay, and system failures, or will it just mask deeper problems that need long-term investment?

## The Road Ahead

AI could reshape health care in Africa over the next decade. Some estimates say it could save up to a million lives by 2030 and bring remote services to hundreds of millions of people. Faster and more precise detection of cancer, malaria, and TB is within reach. Doctors may use genetic data to guide treatment and lean on generative AI to help with complex decisions. Telemedicine will grow stronger through wearables that track vital signs, send early warnings, and make virtual visits easier for people in remote areas. AI can also scan huge data streams, from weather to social media, to spot and predict outbreaks of diseases like Ebola or cholera. Hospitals could use it to manage beds, plan staff needs, and keep medical supplies moving.

Several trends point the way forward. Local developers are working to build tools in African languages and to avoid bias. AI will pair with other technologies such as the Internet of Things and cloud computing. Wider internet access and more smartphones will feed the data these systems need. Investors are paying more attention to African health start-ups, including those led by women.

To make this future real and fair, countries will need to invest in digital infrastructure, train AI specialists, and keep talent on the continent. Strong local rules for data privacy and ethics must guide the work, with people, not just algorithms, making final decisions. Governments, health providers, tech companies, and international partners will have to plan and build together if AI is to deliver lasting gains.

## Conclusion

Artificial intelligence offers Africa a rare chance to skip some of the slow steps that other regions took in building modern health systems. With the right choices, countries can use AI to expand care, cut costs, and reach people long left out of quality treatment.

Success will depend on African leadership and solutions built for local languages, cultures, and realities. Strong ethics and clear rules must guide how data is collected and how decisions are made. Technology can help, but it is only part of the answer.

The continent’s energy and creativity are already driving new ideas and partnerships. If governments, health workers, and innovators stay focused on people as well as tools, Africa can create a future where AI supports, not replaces, the human touch at the heart of care.

## That "Package Tracking" Feeling, but for Your Health

There's a peculiar satisfaction in watching that little dot inch its way across a map, signaling the imminent arrival of a pizza or that long-awaited package. But what if that same granular visibility, that same sense of control, extended to something far more critical: life-saving medicines and vaccines?

It's no longer a futuristic fantasy. An invisible, high-tech network quietly orchestrates the movement of pharmaceuticals across the globe, proving itself an unsung hero, especially during the recent pandemic. The magic relies on three key pillars: complete supply-chain visibility, super-smart route optimization that considers far more than mere distance, and proactive stock management, ensuring that critical supplies are always within reach.

## A Quick History Lesson: We’ve Come a Long Way from "Arm-to-Arm"

Let's rewind a bit. Imagine a time when medical logistics involved monks carefully transporting medicinal herbs between monasteries, or even the early days of vaccines, where they were literally carried "arm-to-arm" to maintain their efficacy.

The Industrial Revolution brought trains and steamships, offering a significant leap in speed and scale. The 20th century introduced refrigeration, birthing the "cold chain," and saw the rise of first-generation computers – those room-sized IBM behemoths – used for rudimentary inventory management. Then came the "Just-in-Time" era, a philosophy of efficiency and leanness that, while ground-breaking, proved remarkably fragile when faced with unforeseen global disruptions.

## The Modern Toolkit: What's Powering the Medical Supply Chain 2.0?

We've entered a new era of digital transformation. Let's dissect the tools that are revolutionizing medical logistics:

- **The "Where's My Pizza?" Tracker for Pills (Supply-Chain Visibility):** Forget static location data. We're talking about an intricate web of IoT sensors, GPS, and RFID tags, meticulously monitoring not just *where* a shipment is, but its precise temperature, humidity, and even potential shocks it may encounter. This granular level of insight eliminates guesswork, ensuring that vaccines, for instance, haven't been compromised by temperature fluctuations.
- **The Ultimate GPS on Steroids (Route Optimization):** Today's route optimization goes far beyond finding the shortest path. Sophisticated AI algorithms analyze a multitude of factors, including real-time traffic conditions, weather patterns, delivery time windows, and even geopolitical events, to dynamically calculate the *smartest* path. This saves time, reduces fuel consumption, minimizes the risk of delays, and ultimately, saves lives.
- **The End of "Sorry, We're Out" (Real-time Stock Management):** Digital systems are actively working to eradicate stockouts and minimize waste. AI algorithms predict demand spikes, such as during flu season, and automate reorders proactively. Consider India's Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network (eVIN), a real-world example of digitizing vaccine stocks to ensure availability and prevent spoilage.

## The Controversy Corner: It's Not All Smooth Sailing

It’s crucial to acknowledge the complexities and potential pitfalls of this technological revolution. It's not a panacea.

- **The Digital Divide:** The most advanced technology is rendered useless when faced with fundamental infrastructure gaps. An ultra-cold freezer is of little value in an area with an unreliable power grid. The success of digital logistics hinges on the strength of the underlying infrastructure.
- **Data, Data, Everywhere... But is it Safe?** The vast amounts of data generated by these systems raise critical questions about privacy and security. The threat of cyberattacks targeting the cold chain is very real, and regulations like GDPR highlight the importance of safeguarding sensitive information.
- **Ethical Speed Bumps:** Algorithmic decision-making introduces ethical dilemmas. Who gets priority access to vaccines? How do we ensure that the algorithms guiding these decisions are free from bias and promote equitable access for all? This is a global debate with no easy answers.

## Peeking into the Future: What's Next on the Horizon?

The future of medical logistics holds incredible promise:

- **Digital Twins:** The creation of virtual replicas of entire supply chains allows us to simulate "what-if" scenarios and proactively identify potential vulnerabilities before a crisis even emerges.
- **Drone Delivery:** Delivering critical supplies to remote, hard-to-reach areas in a matter of minutes, bypassing traditional logistical bottlenecks.
- **"Super Automation":** Imagine a supply chain that is virtually self-managing, autonomously predicting disruptions and rerouting shipments with minimal human intervention.

The ultimate goal is the creation of a resilient, adaptive healthcare system prepared to meet any challenge, anywhere in the world.

## The Takeaway:

Digital logistics forms the invisible yet indispensable infrastructure underpinning modern medicine. We've evolved from a simple chain of delivery trucks to an intelligent, interconnected, and resilient global health network. It ensures that treatments, vaccines, and life-saving medicines reach those who need them, precisely when they need them, solidifying its status as the silent guardian of global health.
